bib.title: On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification". Qinyuan Ye, Yu Li, Yada Pruksachatkun, Jiaxin Zhang, Chien-Sheng Wu (Salesforce AI Research). arXiv 2608.18066v2 [cs.AI], dated 6 Sep 2026 (the arXiv ID implies v1 in Aug 2026). The paper is marked "Preprint", but it carries a NeurIPS checklist. First author month/year: Ye, Sep 2026 for v2. Code: github Salesforce/self-improve-fragility.

COVERAGE: 32 pages, 105,017 chars. I read chars 0-84,000 in full. That covers the main text, references, limitations, appendices A-G, and the start of the NeurIPS checklist. I skimmed the tail (chars 84,000 to the end). It is the Table 16 remainder plus boilerplate NeurIPS checklist, with no results. Page numbers below are approximate, taken from page markers in the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Memory-based self-improvement often fails to beat a no-memory baseline once the base agent is strong, and the one apparent gain is not significant.
  number: ReasoningBank (RBank) +1.5 points on WebArena, Welch p=0.23 (3 runs). AWM -0.7. At n=6 runs, p=0.07 (still not significant).
  setup: GPT-5-mini agent, WebArena 812 tasks, default task order, ground-truth reward given to the memory builder.
  quote: "although RBank achieves an average improvement of 1.5% over the no-memory baseline, a two-sided Welch's t-test on three runs gives p= 0.23, indicating that the gain is not statistically significant"
  where: p4; n=6 result in §E, p19
- Claim: Shuffling task order turns the claimed improvement into a degradation.
  number: Default order +1.5%; shuffled orders -4.5% (abstract average). WebArena Shuffle-1: baseline 54.8 -> AWM 49.1, RBank 49.8. Degradation is significant in 6 of 8 cases.
  setup: WebArena and VisualWebArena, GPT-5-mini, AWM and RBank, 3 runs each, two random shuffles.
  quote: "when evaluated under a shuffled task order, agent performance degrades (-4.5%) instead of exhibiting the expected improvement (+1.5%)." and "Model performance degrade significantly in 6 out of 8 cases when shuffled orders are used."
  where: abstract p1; Fig 3 p6
- Claim: The default benchmark order is an implicit easy-to-hard curriculum, a hidden prerequisite for the methods to work.
  number: Moving-average pass rate starts near 75% and falls below 40% after task ID 150 (Shopping Admin, GitLab).
  setup: No-memory baseline, window=30, GPT-5-mini.
  quote: "the curves begin with high pass rates (around 75%), which subsequently decline to below 40% once the task ID exceeds 150."
  where: §3.3, p5; Fig 2 p6
- Claim: Self-improving loops amplify run-to-run variance. Even the no-memory baseline is noisy.
  number: Variance rises in 17 of 24 cases (~71%); 11 cases rise by more than 50%. GitLab best-worst gap is 4.4 points for the baseline and 7.8 for RBank. Largest gaps: 8.2 on Map, 10.4 on Multisite. Largest std is 3.9 (up to 4.28 on Multisite). Baseline gap reaches 6.7 on SCUBA Service.
  setup: 3 identical runs per setting, GPT-5-mini, default order, 11 domains across WebArena, VisualWebArena and SCUBA, std of pass@1 across runs.
  quote: "In 17 of the 24 cases, we see an increase in variances, and in 11 cases the relative increase exceeds 50%."
  where: §3.2, p4; Table 1 p5
- Claim: Cause given for the amplification is statefulness. Early randomness compounds into different memory states.
  number: none
  setup: Authors' explanation, not an ablation.
  quote: "memory construction is conditioned on prior task outcomes and is further influenced by stochastic LLM sampling. As a result, early randomness can compound over time"
  where: p4
- Claim: Three runs understate the spread. Going to six widens it.
  number: Shopping gap for RBank 3.21 -> 8.02 (n=3 -> n=6). RBank std is larger than baseline in 5 of 6 domains at n=6.
  setup: WebArena, ordinal order, baseline and RBank, GPT-5-mini.
  quote: "best-worst gaps grow in most domains (e.g., shopping: 3.21→8.02 for ReasoningBank), indicating that n=3 may understate the true variability"
  where: §E, p19
- Claim: Memories are unverified hypotheses. They can be plausible but inapplicable, and they cascade.
  number: "user confirmation" appears in memory 26 times (3 WebArena runs) and 22 times (3 VisualWebArena runs). API mentions recur across domains (Fig 4).
  setup: Manual, qualitative inspection of RBank memories. The memory writer was not told the environment is browser-only with no code and no human-confirmation channel.
  quote: "without proper validation mechanisms, agent memories are merely unverified hypotheses rather than true lessons learned."
  where: §4.1 p6-7; Conclusion p9
- Claim: A fallback that happened to score became a reinforced strategy. This is reward-hacking-like and contagious. The earlier "Haversine" enters memory, the more it is retrieved later.
  number: none (Fig 4c shows keyword counts)
  setup: WebArena map domain, travel-time tasks. Task 38 passed because the answer contained "yes" while the route was estimated by the haversine formula (Table 16).
  quote: "the earlier "Haversine" is added to memory, the more frequently it is retrieved and used in later tasks."
  where: p7; Table 16 p25
- Claim: The verifier itself can poison the loop. Ambiguous tasks and evaluator bugs generate spurious memories.
  number: none
  setup: WebArena task 118 (jaw bruxism) was answered as Q&A, and the memory said "gather targeted patient/context details". Task 329: "0.00" is judged not equal to "0", a false negative that produced an irrelevant memory.
  quote: "benchmark evaluator bugs lead to false negatives during evaluation, which in turn cause the agent to overthink and generate spurious memories."
  where: p7; Tables 14-15 p24
- Claim: Giving the memory writer more specification (rubrics, environment feedback, a prompt that forbids unsupported strategies) recovers only part of the loss.
  number: Shuffle-1 RBank 49.8 -> 52.7 (+2.9) with all three; +1.1 on Shuffle-2; default order unchanged (56.3). This closes 31% of the degradation, leaving 69%. Singles: +Rub 52.3, +Env 50.9, +PMod 50.9. The agent still underperforms the baseline (54.8) on both shuffles.
  setup: RBank on WebArena, GPT-5-mini. Rubrics and scores are shown only to the memory builder, not to the agent during the task. The prompt edit says "STRICTLY AVOID: API or programmatic solutions, visiting external websites, requesting human confirmation".
  quote: "These interventions close 31% of the performance degradation observed in the shuffled task order settings."
  where: Intro p2; §4.2 p7-8; Fig 5 p8; Table 4 p7
- Claim: Findings hold partly across models and a third, filesystem-based method.
  number: GPT-OSS-120B shuffled 37.0 vs 40.6 baseline; Gemini-2.5-Pro shuffled 48.0 vs 49.1; Gemini RBank Shuffle-1 GitLab gap 9.4, GPT-OSS Reddit gap 13.2. EnterpriseOps-Gym with memory: 24.5->22.3 (GPT-OSS-120B), 30.5->29.7 (GPT-5.4-mini). More variance in 10 of 16 domain cases. Drive gap 4.7 -> 14.1.
  setup: Letta Code reflection agent that edits files, skills and system prompts. Binary reward is revealed. 3 runs.
  caveat: Variance amplification is model-dependent. RBank std rises in 8/12 (GPT-5-mini), 7/12 (GPT-OSS), 5/12 (Gemini). The authors call the evidence weaker for the latter two.
  quote: "the overall success rate drops slightly with memory enabled (24.5→22.3 for GPT-OSS-120B; 30.5→29.7 for GPT-5.4-mini)."
  where: §E p19-20; Tables 12-13
- Claim: A strong base model removes most of what memory previously added.
  number: Prior RBank paper: Gemini-2.5-Pro 46.7 -> 53.9 on 684 tasks. Here the no-memory GPT-5-mini baseline scores 55.3 on the same set. On the full 812 tasks: 54.8. VisualWebArena baseline 54.9 (leaderboard best 54.0 as of 1 May 2026). Memory deltas: SCUBA AWM -1.7, RBank +1.4.
  quote: "Our baseline agent, based on the more recent GPT-5-mini model, achieves comparable performance (55.3%) to their reported memory-enabled result (53.9%)."
  where: p4 Tables 2-3
- Claim: Per-task reliability is low even without memory.
  number: WebArena pass@3 65.4 vs pass^3 43.3; VWA 66.3 vs 42.4; SCUBA 43.8 vs 15.4. The gap often exceeds 20 points.
  setup: No-memory baseline, GPT-5-mini. Not applicable to self-improving runs, because tasks are state-dependent within a run.
  quote: "the gap between pass@3 and passˆ3 frequently exceeds 20%."
  where: Appendix D, p17 Tables 5-6
- Claim: A proper protocol is expensive.
  number: ~$25 per WebArena run (812 tasks), ~$29 per SCUBA run (267 tasks), baseline only. Pass@3 per run across 3 runs would cost 9x the single-run protocol.
  quote: "a single run over all 812 WebArena tasks costs around $25"
  where: Appendix C p16; D.2 p17

Recommendations (p9)
- Report multiple self-improving runs and randomized task orders.
- Pilot on well-specified tasks, then stress-test on underspecified ones to estimate worst-case behaviour.
- Add memory validation that filters bad memories.
- Provide interfaces for human oversight and timely intervention, because deployment is a single irreversible run.

LIMITS
- Scope is web-browsing benchmarks and mostly GPT-5-mini. The core analysis covers two memory methods that store text only, with no weight updates. It is inference-only. Newer memory techniques were not evaluated.
- Memory inspection was qualitative and covered a subset of memories.
- Underspecification explains only part of the loss. The remaining 69% is uncharacterized.
- Ground-truth reward was given to the memory builder, rather than a noisy LLM-judge proxy. Real loops with proxy rewards would likely be worse; the paper does not test this.
- Only 3 runs (6 in one experiment), and the n=3 spread is shown to be understated.
- Shuffled-order degradation is mostly a WebArena finding. In VisualWebArena, RBank is less sensitive (56.0 and 56.4 under shuffle vs 55.6 default), while AWM drops.
- Variance amplification is weaker for other models (see the GPT-OSS and Gemini counts above).
- Models and benchmark leaderboard numbers are dated 2026.

BUILDS ON
- Agent Workflow Memory, Wang et al. 2025 (ICML). ReasoningBank, Ouyang et al. 2025. Synapse, Zheng et al. 2024 (SCUBA table).
- Benchmarks: WebArena (Zhou et al. 2024), VisualWebArena (Koh et al. 2024), SCUBA (Dai et al. 2025), EnterpriseOps-Gym (Malay et al. 2026).
- Harnesses: WALT (Prabhu et al. 2026), Letta Code (Packer et al. 2023; Lin et al. 2025 on sleep-time compute).
- Reliability framing: Rabanser et al. 2026, "Towards a science of AI agent reliability". Also pass^k from tau-bench (Yao et al. 2024).
- WebArena Verified (El hattami et al. 2025), on ambiguous tasks.
- Self-improvement lineage: Gödel machines (Schmidhuber 2006), STaR (Zelikman 2022), Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al. 2026), ADAS (Hu et al. 2025), Huxley-Gödel Machine.
- Monitorability: Baker et al. 2025 (reward hacking via CoT monitoring).
- Stability literature: Henderson et al. 2019 (deep RL that matters).

CODE: no runnable code. Verbatim prompt fragments worth keeping:
- RBank generic memory prompt, Listing 2, p22: "You need to extract and summarize useful insights in the format of memory items based on the agent's successful trajectory." It also says "You can extract at most 3 memory items from the trajectory." and "Do not mention specific websites, queries, or string contents". Neither the generic prompt nor the failed-trajectory prompt (Listing 3, p23) mentions the environment's constraints.
- +PMod, Table 4, p7: "STRICTLY AVOID: API or programmatic solutions, visiting external websites, requesting human confirmation, or task-specific details tied to a particular site or query."
- +Rub example, Table 4: "Evaluator: string_match | Score: 0.0 (FAIL) ... must_include: ... →PASS / →FAIL".

FIGURES (captions confirmed from the extraction; I did not run the figures script)
- Fig 1, p3: memory-based self-improvement loop plus AWM and RBank example memories. It shows the task -> memory -> bank -> retriever loop at a glance.
- Fig 2, p6: moving-average pass rate by task ID in the default order. It makes the implicit curriculum visible.
- Fig 3, p6: pass rate by order (default, Shuffle-1, Shuffle-2) for AWM and RBank against the baseline. This is the headline "gain flips to loss" chart.
- Fig 4, p7: keyword mentions ("API", "Haversine") in retrieved memory across completed tasks, per run. It shows a bad memory spreading.
- Fig 5, p8: ablation of +Rub, +Env, +PMod, +All, and the effect across task orders.
- Table 1, p5: variance table for all 11 domains. Tables 5-6 give the pass@3 vs pass^3 gap.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean text, with figure axes garbled but captions readable. The first-page version marker is v2, and v1's date is unknown. Section "§4.1" and "§4.2" page numbers are approximate. The bibliography has some oddities ("2026" conference years for NeurIPS 2025 items), which I did not use.
